analysis.one_liner: Requires phone companies to give customers free caller-ID verification and robocall blocking, and bans spoofed calls from abroad.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 22 House sponsors and cosponsors, the bill never left the Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a House vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The ROBOCOP Act would extend the ban on fake caller ID to callers overseas and to text messages, and it would require phone companies, at no extra charge, to give customers tools that verify caller ID and flag or block robocalls — with exceptions for public safety calls and calls a customer agreed to receive. It also lets people sue companies that violate the rules and penalizes anyone who deliberately breaks call-blocking technology. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary phone customers, especially older people targeted by phone scams, who would get free tools to verify who is really calling and to block robot and recorded calls. The bill cites 3.5 million complaints about unwanted calls to the Federal Trade Commission in 2015 and an estimated $350 million annual cost to consumers [S3]. It also protects domestic violence shelters and medical practices that legitimately need to mask their numbers, by giving them an exemption process [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires originating phone providers to verify, at no extra charge, that the caller ID shown for a call accurately identifies the caller, closing a loophole for calls made from outside the United States to U.S. recipients and for spoofed text messages [S2][S3].

Requires receiving providers to offer, free of charge, technology that flags and blocks calls from automatic dialing systems and prerecorded voices, while exempting public safety agencies and calls the subscriber previously consented to receive [S2][S3].

Creates a private right of action letting people recover $500 per violation (up to triple for willful violations) and lets state attorneys general sue over a pattern of failing to provide the required technology [S2][S3].

Includes an exemption process for callers with legitimate needs to mask their numbers, such as domestic violence shelters and medical practices, and an appeals process for callers wrongly labeled as robocallers [S2][S3].
Makes it unlawful to intentionally interfere with call-blocking technology, for example by causing it to wrongly block a public safety call [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telephone and internet-calling providers, which would have to build and offer verification and blocking technology to every subscriber at no additional charge, and businesses that rely on outbound automated calling, whose legitimate calls could be flagged or blocked pending appeal [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Phone companies would bear the cost of building and maintaining call-verification and call-blocking technology for all subscribers at no extra charge, a cost that could be recovered through rates or reduced investment [S2][S3].

Legitimate automated callers, such as businesses making appointment reminders or debt collection calls, could see their calls mislabeled and blocked; the bill answers this with an appeals process and consent exceptions, but the friction is real [S3].
The bill relies on the FCC to write detailed technical standards within 18 months, and disputes over those standards could delay relief for consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is substantial and direct: verified caller ID and free robocall blocking attack a problem the bill's own findings peg at 3.5 million complaints a year. The main cost falls on phone providers, who would have to provide the technology for free, and on legitimate mass callers facing possible mislabeling — real, but modest next to the consumer protection, and partly mitigated by the bill's exemption and appeal processes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, never received a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the ROBOCOP Act on April 13, 2016, with Reps. Steve Cohen and Chris Van Hollen as original cosponsors [S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 13, 2016, and to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on April 15, 2016 [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never advanced out of committee or subcommittee, never received a House floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].
All 21 cosponsors were House Democrats; no House Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone companies avoided a mandate to provide free call-verification and blocking technology, and operations making spoofed or automated scam calls faced no new penalties from this bill. Consumers remained exposed to the unwanted and fraudulent calls the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 21 cosponsors were House Democrats; no House Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would require these companies to build and offer caller-ID verification and robocall-blocking technology to every subscriber at no additional charge, plus report and comply with FCC standards. Their interest in avoiding that unfunded mandate ran against customers' interest in free protection, though a functioning blocking system would also cut fraud costs for the networks.

The bill targets exactly this business model: it extends the spoofing ban to calls from abroad and to texts, requires the technology that flags robot calls, and adds $500-per-violation private lawsuits and state enforcement. The bill died, so these operations continued unimpeded by it.

Hospitals, debt collectors, and other legitimate automated callers could see their calls mislabeled and blocked by the required consumer tools, hurting their ability to reach people. The bill mitigates this with an appeals process, a consent exception, and exemptions for callers with legitimate needs.
